examples.problem_statement: For the integers a, b, and c, the sum of a and b is 75% of c. Quantity A: (3/4)(a + b). Quantity B: (4/3)(c). Compare the two quantities.

solution.result: a constraint linking a, b and c that any test values must satisfy
solution.description: Write the given condition as an equation: the sum of a and b equals 75% of c. Every set of numbers you try later has to obey this.

solution.result: a valid positive test case, in which Quantity B is greater
solution.description: Pick positive integers that satisfy the constraint. The book notes these are valid because 1 + 2 is 75% of 4, and with all variables positive Quantity B comes out greater.

solution.result: an equally valid negative test case, in which Quantity A is greater
solution.description: Pick negative integers that also satisfy the constraint. Nothing in the problem rules out negatives, and with negative variables the comparison flips so that Quantity A is greater.

solution.result: opposite outcomes from two legal cases, so no fixed relationship holds
solution.description: Set the two results side by side. Because one legal set of values makes B greater and another makes A greater, the relationship is not determined by the given information.

key_reminders: The variables are only said to be integers, so negative values and zero must be tested, not just positives.
Any test values you pick must still satisfy the stated condition a + b = 75% of c.
In quantitative comparison, two admissible cases with opposite outcomes force the 'cannot be determined' answer.
common_mistakes: Testing only positive numbers such as a = 1, b = 2, c = 4 and concluding Quantity B is greater.
Reading 'integers' as 'positive integers' and never trying a = -1, b = -2, c = -4.

concept.technique_name: digit-count ranges in a given base

examples.problem_statement: What is the difference between the highest and the least 4-digit natural numbers that have exactly 4 digits when expressed in Base 6 and Base 7.

solution.description: Write the range of numbers that have 4 digits in the decimal system: from 10 cubed up to one less than 10 to the fourth.
Apply the same rule in Base 7: a 4-digit Base 7 number runs from 7 cubed up to one less than 7 to the fourth.
Do it once more in Base 6: a 4-digit Base 6 number runs from 6 cubed up to one less than 6 to the fourth.
Overlap the three ranges to keep only the numbers common to all of them. The largest lower bound is 1000 and the smallest upper bound is 1295.
Subtract the least common value from the highest common value to get the required difference.

key_reminders: A number has exactly 4 digits in base b when it lies from b^3 up to b^4 - 1.
'Common to all bases' means intersecting the ranges: take the largest lower bound and the smallest upper bound.
common_mistakes: Using 6^4 and 7^4 as the upper limits instead of 6^4 - 1 = 1295 and 7^4 - 1 = 2400.
Forgetting the decimal 4-digit condition and starting the overlap at 343 instead of 1000.

examples.problem_statement: If the average of x and y is 50, and the average of y and z is 80, what is the value of z - x ?

solution.description: Use the rule that the sum of two numbers is twice their average on the pair x and y, then isolate x.
Apply the same rule to the pair y and z, then isolate z so both unknowns are written in terms of y.
Substitute these two expressions into the quantity being asked for, z minus x.
Expand the subtraction and simplify. The y terms cancel, leaving a plain numerical difference.

solution.operation: \text{Smart Numbers: } x = 50,\ y = 50 \Rightarrow z = 160 - 50 = 110,\ z - x = 110 - 50
solution.description: Check the result the book's alternative way: choose x = 50 and y = 50 so their average is 50, force y + z = 160 to get z = 110, and take the difference.

key_reminders: The sum of two numbers is twice their average.
Writing both x and z in terms of y lets y cancel, so no individual value is ever needed.
Smart Numbers work here only if the chosen values satisfy both average conditions.
common_mistakes: Dropping the parentheses in (160 - y) - (100 - y) so the y terms do not cancel.
Trying to solve for x, y and z individually when the system has infinitely many solutions and only z - x is fixed.
